Summary

Das and Menon describe an analysis of a large open-source iEEG dataset (UPENN-RAM). From encoding and recall phases of memory tasks, they analyzed power and phase-transfer entropy as a measure of directed information flow in regions across a hypothesized tripartite network system. The anterior insula (AI) was found to have heightened high gamma power during encoding and retrieval, which corresponded to suppression of high gamma power in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) during encoding but not recall. In contrast, directed information flow from (but not to) AI to mPFC and PCC is high during both time periods when PTE is analyzed with broadband but not narrowband activity. They claim that these findings significantly advance an understanding of how network communication facilitates cognitive operations during memory tasks, and that the AI of the salience network (SN) is responsible for influencing both the frontoparietal network (FPN) and default-mode network (DMN) during memory encoding and retrieval.

I find this question interesting and important and agree with the authors that iEEG presents a unique opportunity to investigate the temporal dynamics within network nodes. Their findings convey intriguing information about the structure and order of communication between network regions during on-task cognition in general (though, perhaps not specific to memory - see Weaknesses), with the AI of the SN ostensibly playing an important role in possibly influencing the DMN and FPN.

Strengths

- The authors present results from an impressively-sized iEEG sample. For reader context, this type of invasive human data is difficult and time-consuming to collect and many similar studies in high-level journals include 5-20 participants, typically not all of whom have electrodes in all regions of interest. It is excellent that they have been able to leverage open-source data in this way.

- Preprocessing of iEEG data also seems sensible and appropriate based on field standards.

- The authors tackle the replication issues inherent in much of the literature by replicating findings across task contexts, demonstrating that the principles of network communication evidenced by their results generalize in multiple task memory contexts. Again, the number of iEEG patients who have multiple tasks' worth of data is impressive.

- Though the revised manuscript presents a broader and more novel investigation of the tripartite network's role in memory encoding and retrieval (as opposed to cognitive control of memory) the authors now thoroughly review the literature motivating this investigation of open-source data.

Weaknesses

- As the authors discuss, it is currently unclear if the directed information flow from AI to DMN and FPN nodes truly arises from memory-associated processes as opposed to more general attentional and cognitive demands, especially given that information flow does not relate meaningfully to task performance (whether memory retrieval is successful or not). I also note this is a concern because - though the authors have now demonstrated that information flow is increased compared to an off-task baseline - influences of AI on DMN or FPN were not increased relative to baseline epochs during the task in the original preprint version, again suggesting these effects may not be specific to the memory component of the analyzed tasks. The authors have thoughtfully noted in the Discussion several ways that experimental design can be improved in future studies to address this limitation.

results.result: The anterior insula (AI) exerts consistently higher directed information flow to both DMN and FPN nodes compared to the reverse direction during both memory encoding and recall. This pattern was replicated across all four memory experiments (VFR, CATVFR, PALVCR, WMSM) with very high Bayes factors (BF > 10^4 in most cases), and was significantly stronger during memory tasks compared to resting state baseline.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C7, C30-C45, C50-C51, C53-C57 provide converging evidence from phase transfer entropy (PTE) analyses showing consistent directional information flow from AI to DMN/FPN nodes. The findings are supported by detailed statistical tests (F-statistics, p-values, Cohen's d), high Bayes replication factors across multiple experiments, and task vs. rest comparisons. The net outflow analyses (C53-C57) further confirm the AI's role as an outflow hub.

results.result: High-gamma power in the PCC/precuneus was suppressed compared to the AI during memory encoding across all four tasks, but this suppression was absent during recall. The AI showed enhanced high-gamma power compared to baseline during both encoding and recall, while PCC/precuneus showed reduced power compared to baseline during encoding in three tasks (VFR, PALVCR, WMSM).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C21-C29 demonstrate task-specific high-gamma suppression in PCC/precuneus during encoding with statistical support (ps<0.05) and replication across experiments (BF 5.16e+1 and 2.69e+8). The differential pattern between encoding and recall is consistently observed, and baseline comparisons provide additional validation. The findings are supported by Figure 3 showing temporal dynamics.

results.result: Control analyses using the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) showed an inverse pattern to the AI, with DMN and FPN exerting higher influence on IFG than the reverse. The AI's net outflow was significantly higher than IFG's during both encoding and recall across all four experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C46-C49 provide critical control analyses demonstrating the specificity of AI's role. The inverse pattern in IFG (C48) and significantly higher net outflow from AI compared to IFG (C49, ps<0.001 across all experiments) strengthen the interpretation that AI's outflow hub role is not simply due to anatomical location or general cognitive control functions.

results.result: No significant differences in directed influence from AI to DMN/FPN were found between successfully recalled and forgotten memory trials during encoding or recall in any of the four memory experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 reports a null finding with appropriate statistical testing (ps>0.05) across all experiments. While this is a negative result, it is clearly stated and appropriately analyzed, suggesting the observed network dynamics may reflect general attentional or cognitive processes rather than memory-specific encoding/retrieval success.

results.result: Narrowband phase locking values (PLV) did not significantly differ between encoding/recall and rest periods in any frequency band (delta-theta, alpha, beta, gamma, high-gamma), suggesting that PTE rather than phase synchronization captures AI dynamic interactions with DMN and FPN.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 report null findings for PLV analyses across multiple frequency bands, supporting the interpretation that broadband PTE is more sensitive than narrowband phase synchronization for detecting network interactions. This methodological finding justifies the analytical approach used throughout the study.

results.result: The study analyzed iEEG data from 177 participants (out of 249 initially available) across four episodic memory experiments (VFR, CATVFR, PALVCR, WMSM) from the UPENN-RAM dataset, with electrode coverage in AI, DMN nodes (PCC/precuneus, mPFC), and FPN nodes (dPPC, MFG). Behavioral performance showed recall accuracies ranging from 25-48% across tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C60-C61, C65-C75 provide comprehensive description of the dataset, participant selection criteria, task designs, and behavioral performance. The sample size is substantial for iEEG studies, electrode coverage is appropriate for testing the triple network model, and behavioral data confirm participants engaged meaningfully with the tasks.

results.result: Phase transfer entropy (PTE) was selected as the primary analytical method because it can handle nonlinear and nonstationary dynamics in iEEG data, unlike Granger causality which requires stationarity. Stationarity testing confirmed iEEG time series were nonstationary. Broadband (0.5-80 Hz) rather than narrowband analysis was used based on nonhuman primate studies suggesting broadband activity governs information flow.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64, C76-C79, C100-C103 provide methodological justification for analytical choices with appropriate citations. The stationarity test (C102) empirically validates the choice of PTE over Granger causality. Anatomical atlas selection and preprocessing steps are clearly described with citations to prior work.

results.result: The triple network model, comprising the salience network (SN/AI), default mode network (DMN), and frontoparietal network (FPN), provides a framework for understanding dynamic interactions between large-scale brain networks during cognitive processes including episodic memory. Each network has distinct functional roles: SN detects salient stimuli, DMN supports internally-focused processes and memory retrieval, and FPN maintains working memory and attentional control.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C18 establish the theoretical framework with extensive citations to prior literature. These are well-established concepts in cognitive neuroscience that provide the foundation for the study's hypotheses. The characterization of each network's function is consistent with the broader literature.

results.result: High-gamma activity (80-160 Hz) is correlated with fMRI BOLD signals, reflects local neuronal activity, and has been implicated in various cognitive tasks across sensory modalities and cognitive domains including working memory and episodic memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20, C80-C81 describe established properties of high-gamma activity with appropriate citations. This background knowledge justifies the use of high-gamma power as a measure of local neural activity in the study.

results.result: The observed PCC/precuneus suppression during encoding likely reflects functional down-regulation to minimize interference from internally-oriented processes during external information encoding. The differential pattern between encoding (externally-driven) and recall (internally-driven) reflects distinct cognitive demands. High-gamma activity reflects localized processing while lower frequencies support longer-range network communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 provide interpretations of the high-gamma findings that are reasonable given the data and consistent with prior literature (with citations). These interpretations connect local activity patterns to broader theories of memory encoding and recall, though they remain somewhat speculative.

results.result: The AI's directed influence on DMN and FPN may reflect a general role in coordinating attentional resources rather than memory-specific processes. Successful memory recall likely involves brain systems beyond the triple network model, including the medial temporal lobe. The persistent AI influence during recall may reflect ongoing monitoring of retrieved information, though PTE analysis at ~2s timescales may miss subtle dynamics during recall initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 acknowledge important limitations and alternative interpretations with appropriate citations. The authors appropriately note that their findings may not be memory-specific (C87), that other brain systems are involved (C88-C89), and that methodological constraints may limit detection of rapid dynamics (C92). These represent honest assessments of the study's scope.

results.result: The findings align with prior work showing AI has higher controllability compared to DMN/FPN nodes, positioning it to dynamically engage/disengage with other brain areas. The results provide a novel neurophysiological perspective on the Atkinson and Shiffrin memory model, with PCC/precuneus suppression and AI enhancement during encoding potentially reflecting control processes regulating information transitions across memory stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 connect the current findings to prior theoretical frameworks (controllability theory, Atkinson-Shiffrin model) with appropriate citations. These interpretations are reasonable extensions of the data, though they remain somewhat speculative (C98-C99 are explicitly interpretive).

results.result: The study extends the applicability of the triple network model beyond cognitive control tasks to episodic memory processes, advancing understanding of the SN's role in modulating large-scale brain networks during memory formation and underscoring the model's importance in domain-general coordination of brain networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 represent the authors' summary of the study's contributions. These are supported by the convergent findings from multiple experiments showing consistent AI-directed influences during memory tasks. The extension to episodic memory represents a meaningful advance given the model was primarily developed in cognitive control contexts.

results.result: The anterior insula (AI) shows consistently higher directed information flow to both DMN (PCC/precuneus, mPFC) and FPN (dPPC, MFG) nodes during both memory encoding and recall phases. This directed influence is significantly stronger during memory tasks compared to resting state, and the pattern persists across externally driven encoding and internally governed recall. The AI functions as an outflow hub with very high Bayes replication factors across all four experiments.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge these findings as 'valuable' and 'convincing,' they express significant concern that the directed information flow may not be specific to memory processes. The reviewer notes that 'it is currently unclear if the directed information flow from AI to DMN and FPN nodes truly arises from memory-associated processes as opposed to more general attentional and cognitive demands,' especially since information flow does not relate to task performance (successful vs. forgotten trials). The reviewer also notes concern that in the original preprint, AI influences were not increased relative to baseline during tasks, 'again suggesting these effects may not be specific to the memory component.'

results.result: Task-specific suppression of high-gamma power in the PCC/precuneus node of the DMN was observed during memory encoding but not recall, while AI high-gamma power was increased during both phases. This differential pattern was replicated across multiple tasks with high Bayes factors, and PCC/precuneus activity was reduced compared to resting baseline in three tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about the high-gamma power findings. The editor's summary describes the findings as 'valuable' and the analyses as 'convincing,' and the anonymous reviewer lists the replication across task contexts as a strength, noting the authors 'demonstrate that the principles of network communication evidenced by their results generalize in multiple task memory contexts.' The differential encoding vs. recall pattern is not specifically challenged.

results.result: Control analyses using the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) showed an inverse pattern compared to AI, with DMN and FPN exerting higher influence on IFG than the reverse. The AI's net outflow was significantly higher than IFG during both encoding and recall phases across all four experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the IFG control analyses. The editor describes the overall analyses as 'convincing,' and the anonymous reviewer does not raise methodological concerns about the control region approach. The inverse pattern with IFG is presented as supporting evidence for AI's unique role, and this interpretation is not disputed.

results.result: Analysis did not reveal differences in directed influence from the AI on the DMN and FPN between successfully recalled and forgotten memory trials during encoding or recall periods in any of the memory experiments.
results.evaluation: This null finding is explicitly highlighted by the reviewer as a major concern. The reviewer states that 'information flow does not relate meaningfully to task performance (whether memory retrieval is successful or not)' and uses this as evidence that 'it is currently unclear if the directed information flow from AI to DMN and FPN nodes truly arises from memory-associated processes as opposed to more general attentional and cognitive demands.' This lack of relationship to memory performance undermines claims about memory-specific mechanisms.

results.result: The study analyzed intracranial EEG recordings from 177 participants across four diverse episodic memory experiments (VFR, CATVFR, PALVCR, WMSM) spanning verbal and spatial memory domains. Results were replicated across all experiments with high Bayes replication factors, with substantial participant overlap across tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the dataset and replication approach. The editor 'commend[s] the use of a large intracranial EEG dataset,' and the anonymous reviewer states 'The authors present results from an impressively-sized iEEG sample' and notes 'It is excellent that they have been able to leverage open-source data in this way.' The reviewer also highlights as a strength that 'The authors tackle the replication issues inherent in much of the literature by replicating findings across task contexts' and that 'the number of iEEG patients who have multiple tasks' worth of data is impressive.'

results.result: Narrowband phase-locking value (PLV) analysis did not show significant differences between encoding/recall versus rest periods in any frequency band (delta-theta, alpha, beta, gamma, high-gamma). The authors conclude that phase transfer entropy (PTE), rather than phase synchronization, more robustly captures AI dynamic interactions with DMN and FPN.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the PLV findings or the interpretation that PTE is more appropriate than phase synchronization measures. The methodological choice of PTE is not questioned, and the anonymous reviewer notes that 'Preprocessing of iEEG data also seems sensible and appropriate based on field standards,' which would encompass the connectivity analysis approach.

results.result: The study employed phase transfer entropy (PTE) as a measure of directed information flow, justified by its ability to capture nonlinear and nonstationary dynamics in iEEG data. Stationarity testing confirmed iEEG time series were nonstationary, precluding Granger causality analysis. Broadband (0.5-80 Hz) rather than narrowband analysis was used based on recent evidence that broadband field potentials govern information flow.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about the PTE methodology or the justification for its use. The anonymous reviewer explicitly states 'Preprocessing of iEEG data also seems sensible and appropriate based on field standards,' which encompasses the analytical approach. The methodological choices regarding frequency bands and connectivity measures are not challenged.

results.result: The authors claim the study extends the triple network model to episodic memory processes and significantly advances understanding of the SN's role in modulating large-scale networks during memory formation. However, they acknowledge limitations: the AI's influence may reflect general attentional coordination rather than memory-specific processes, and PTE at ~2s timescales may miss subtle dynamics during internally-driven recall initiation.
results.evaluation: The reviewer directly challenges the memory-specificity of the findings, stating 'it is currently unclear if the directed information flow from AI to DMN and FPN nodes truly arises from memory-associated processes as opposed to more general attentional and cognitive demands.' The reviewer notes the authors 'now thoroughly review the literature motivating this investigation' but emphasizes that findings may convey 'intriguing information about the structure and order of communication between network regions during on-task cognition in general (though, perhaps not specific to memory).' The authors' own acknowledgment of these limitations is noted, with the reviewer stating 'The authors have thoughtfully noted in the Discussion several ways that experimental design can be improved in future studies to address this limitation.'

comparisons.comparison: Both address the core PTE findings showing AI-to-DMN/FPN information flow (C2-C4, C30-C45, C50-C51, C57). OpenEval finds these claims SUPPORTED with strong statistical evidence. Peer reviewers rate them UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the findings as 'valuable' and 'convincing' but expressing significant concern that the directed information flow may reflect general attentional/cognitive demands rather than memory-specific processes, especially given the lack of relationship to task performance.

Perfect agreement on high-gamma suppression findings (C6, C21-C29). Both rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights statistical support and replication across experiments. Peer reviewers do not raise specific concerns, with the editor describing findings as 'valuable' and analyses as 'convincing,' and the reviewer praising replication across task contexts.

Both address IFG control analyses (C5, C48-C49) and agree these are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the inverse pattern in IFG and significantly higher net outflow from AI as strengthening AI's unique role. Peer reviewers do not challenge these control analyses, with the editor describing overall analyses as 'convincing.'

Strong disagreement on the null finding regarding memory performance (C52). OpenEval rates this SUPPORTED as an appropriately reported negative result. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN and explicitly highlight this as a major concern, using the lack of relationship to memory performance as key evidence that the findings may not be memory-specific but rather reflect general cognitive demands.

Perfect agreement on PLV null findings (C58-C59). Both rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval interprets these as justifying the PTE analytical approach. Peer reviewers do not challenge the PLV findings or methodological choice of PTE, with preprocessing and connectivity analysis described as 'sensible and appropriate based on field standards.'

Both address dataset and methodological descriptions (C8, C60-C61, C65-C66, C73-C75) and agree these are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes substantial sample size and appropriate electrode coverage. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the dataset, with the editor commending 'the use of a large intracranial EEG dataset' and the reviewer calling the sample 'impressively-sized' and praising the replication approach.

Strong agreement on methodological justifications (C62-C64, C76-C79, C100-C103). Both rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights appropriate citations and empirical validation of analytical choices. Peer reviewers explicitly state 'Preprocessing of iEEG data also seems sensible and appropriate based on field standards,' encompassing the PTE methodology and justification.

Both address limitations and interpretations (C87-C88, C90, C92), but with different emphasis. OpenEval rates these SUPPORTED as appropriate acknowledgments of limitations. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, directly challenging memory-specificity and emphasizing findings may reflect 'on-task cognition in general (though, perhaps not specific to memory),' while noting the authors 'have thoughtfully noted in the Discussion several ways that experimental design can be improved.'

Both address the study's main conclusions (C104-C106). OpenEval rates these SUPPORTED as meaningful advances extending the triple network model to episodic memory. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning whether findings truly arise from memory-associated processes versus general attentional/cognitive demands, though acknowledging the findings provide 'intriguing information about the structure and order of communication between network regions.'
